_comment: English bodies for langgraph (framework). Mechanism per C0-1..6. Official English quotes kept verbatim. layer_position/providers not rendered — not included.

axes.model_access:
**LangGraph does not touch models at all — a design stance of a low-level framework.**

The five capabilities in the official self-description are
durable execution / HITL / memory / LangSmith debugging / production deployment.
All five are model-agnostic; nowhere is a provider listed.
The official overview files "models" under LangChain:

**Official wording**: "starting with models and tools"

The official overview also states:

**Official wording**: "LangGraph does not abstract prompts or architecture."

Models usually connect via the LangChain integration layer (`init_chat_model` or any SDK).
But the official docs explicitly say it

**Official wording**: "can be used without LangChain"

This line is at the end of the official homepage — **not a hard binding**.

**The official docs provide no provider list — models are simply outside its remit.**
Neither the overview nor the official homepage lists one.

⚠ **Our judgment**: it is not model-bound, and the official homepage has no provider list.
axes.runtime:
**The OSS form is a pure library — no runtime service.**

Installation is just `pip install -U langgraph`.
No CLI to start a service, no container orchestration, no Web UI (the Web UI lives on the Deep Agents / LangSmith side).

**Production deployment points to LangSmith Deployment in the official docs.**
The official overview links **"Production-ready deployment"** to LangSmith Deployment.
That page defines it as:

**Official wording**: "a workflow orchestration runtime purpose-built for agent workloads"

It comes with `langgraph deploy`.
Environments come in four tiers: Cloud / Hybrid / self-hosted K8s / Standalone Agent Server.
Cloud requires **the Plus tier or above**.

**In other words, hosted execution sits at the commercial-platform layer; OSS itself only covers "you run the process yourself".**
axes.local_files:
**⚠ The file system is outside LangGraph's remit.**

The only place the official homepage mentions file systems is recommending Deep Agents as the higher-level package:

**Official wording**: "leverage file systems for complex tasks"

**In other words, file capability is filed under the higher-level wrapper, not the low-level graph engine.**

What LangGraph itself provides is a **state container** — checkpoints store graph state.
Whether the agent reads/writes disks, and with which tools, is not its business.

**Our judgment (inference)**: if you want a file system, wire your own tools.
Or go up to the Deep Agents layer.
axes.background:
**This is its strongest dimension, with explicit official wording.**

The first feature, **Durable execution**, reads verbatim:

Build agents that **persist through failures** and can run for extended periods, **automatically resuming from exactly where they left off**.

The companion is the standalone subpackage `langgraph-checkpoint`.
Check `libs/checkpoint` — the first paragraph of that subpackage's page:

Checkpointers provide a persistence layer for LangGraph: they
**save graph state at every superstep**, enabling
human-in-the-loop, memory between interactions,
**durable execution**, and more.

**The persistence granularity is the superstep (one graph step)** —

not "at session end", not "after each turn"

**The official docs give three persistence backends** (persistence page):

- `InMemorySaver` — stored in RAM; the wording says it
  "does not persist between restarts"

- `SqliteSaver` — local file, for development
- `PostgresSaver` — production; the wording is "In production, use a checkpointer
  backed by a database"

There are also `langgraph-checkpoint-*` implementations for MongoDB / Redis / Oracle.

**Cross-process recovery relies on the database + the same `thread_id`.**
The official durable-execution page says you can
**Official wording**: "resume workflows from the last successful checkpoint"

`langgraph>=1.2` also adds SIGTERM graceful shutdown
(drain, then persist a resumable checkpoint).

**Unknown: conflict semantics of multiple processes writing the same thread concurrently — the official docs do not state it.**
⚠ Neither the persistence nor the checkpointers pages cover this.
axes.tools:
**The LangGraph core contains no tool system, but the official ecosystem has a unified MCP access package.**

None of the five official capabilities is a tool system.
Tools connect via the LangChain ecosystem, or your own functions —
LangGraph handles the graph and state; tools come from LangChain or your functions.

**MCP: the official docs provide `langchain-mcp-adapters`** (the langchain-ai org).
The official homepage says of it

**Official wording**: "makes MCP tools compatible with LangChain and LangGraph"

and **Official wording**: "Convert MCP tools into LangChain tools that can be used with LangGraph agents"

Multiple MCP servers can be connected. **This is the LangChain ecosystem's unified MCP access layer.**

Note it is a standalone package (`pip install langchain-mcp-adapters`), not part of the langgraph core.
axes.context:
**LangGraph splits "state" and "memory" into two mechanisms, both with official wording.**

The third feature, **Comprehensive memory**, reads verbatim:

Create truly stateful agents with both **short-term working memory for ongoing reasoning** and **long-term persistent memory across sessions**.

**Short-term memory**: the official add-memory page gives three trimming techniques —
Trim messages / Delete messages / Summarize messages.
These three are how short context is managed: trim, delete, summarize.
The page positions them as:

**Official wording**: "techniques to manually remove or forget stale information"

**Long-term memory**: a store holding JSON documents.
The official docs say it **supports semantic search and content filtering**:

**Official wording**: "supports both semantic search and filtering by content"

It can recall across threads.

**Unknown: "large tool outputs spilled to disk" — the official docs do not say LangGraph provides it.**
⚠ Neither the memory nor add-memory pages do —
that is the higher-level Deep Agents' context-management capability.
axes.permissions:
**What the official docs give is human-in-the-loop.** It is at the "inspect and modify state" level, not just confirmation.

The second feature, **Human-in-the-loop**, reads verbatim:

Seamlessly incorporate human oversight by **inspecting and modifying agent state at any point during execution**.

The docs are at `langgraph/interrupts`.

**Compared with other listed objects, this point differs substantively.**
The three intervention levels escalate; listed inline because this parser does not support lists inside nested blocks:

- [OpenAI Agents SDK](openai-agents-sdk.md) guardrails **validate content** (are inputs/outputs compliant)
- [Google ADK](google-adk.md) Tool Confirmation **intercepts execution** (should this tool run)
- **LangGraph interrupts modify state** (inspect and modify graph state at any execution point)

⚠ **But say clearly: what it explicitly does not give is a sandbox or permission boundary.**
The official docs mention no file-system permission model, network access control, or tool-level allowlist.
Contrast with OpenHands on our site, which has an explicit Docker sandbox + API-key mechanism.
Also contrast with the Codex SDK (three SandboxMode enum values in source).
**On this dimension, no official mechanism can currently be found for LangGraph.**
axes.fit:
**Four scenarios it fits.**

- Agent flows that run long and must resume precisely from the interruption point
- Human intervention mid-flow that modifies state
- Managing "working memory" and "cross-session long-term memory" separately
- You need an explicit graph structure (branches, loops, subgraphs); your team uses Python

**Three scenarios it does not fit.**

- You need a built-in sandbox or file-level permission boundary — the official docs provide no such mechanism (README and interrupts page checked)
- You want batteries-included file system and subagents — go to Deep Agents, the higher-level package on LangGraph
- You don't want an extra dependency on the LangChain ecosystem — model access usually goes through it

sections.它对「状态」的回答最认真:
Our core claim is "**state ≠ context**".
LangGraph is the only listed object that spells this distinction out on its official homepage.

### Durable execution: persistence granularity is the superstep

The first feature is called **Durable execution**:

> Build agents that **persist through failures**
> and can run for extended periods, **automatically resuming
> from exactly where they left off**.

**"exactly where they left off" is the key.**
Not restarting from scratch — continuing from the interrupted step.

The persistence mechanism lives in the standalone subpackage `langgraph-checkpoint`.
Check `libs/checkpoint` — the first paragraph of that subpackage's page:

> Checkpointers provide a persistence layer for LangGraph: they
> **save graph state at every superstep**, enabling
> human-in-the-loop, memory between interactions,
> **durable execution**, and more.

⚠ **This is the clearest official definition of "state persistence" we have seen.**
The granularity is the **superstep (one graph step)** — not "at session end", not "after each turn".
How we record this granularity: **persistence granularity is the superstep** (one graph step). It is not "at session end". Nor is it "after each turn".

⚠ But honestly: **conflict semantics of cross-machine / multi-process concurrent writes to the same thread are not stated by the official docs**.
The persistence document only gives database backends and durability modes (verified 2026-10-08).

### State and memory: it splits them into two mechanisms

The third feature is called **Comprehensive memory**:

> Create truly stateful agents with both
> **short-term working memory for ongoing reasoning**
> and **long-term persistent memory across sessions**.

**The distinction between two time scales is precisely an isomorphic expression of our claim**:

- checkpoint → stores **flow state** (state plane)
- memory → a separate layer, split into **working memory** and **cross-session long-term memory** (memory plane)

⚠ **The point we most want to stress**: **do not read checkpoint persistence as "context management".**
Checkpoints store graph state.
How long context gets trimmed is the memory layer's business.
The two are strictly recorded apart on this page — which is how the v3 rule "state ≠ context" lands.

⚠ Three items we have not verified:

- exactly how short-term memory trims context (is it compression/summarization?)
- the storage backend and retrieval method of long-term memory
- whether "large tool outputs spilled to disk", which we care about, falls within its capability
sections.HITL 的层次不一样：它能改状态，不只是拦一下:
The second feature **Human-in-the-loop** reads verbatim:

> "Seamlessly incorporate human oversight by
> **inspecting and modifying agent state at any point during execution**."

Putting the three human-intervention mechanisms we have listed side by side, **the levels escalate**:

| Object | Mechanism | Intervention point |
|---|---|---|
| OpenAI Agents SDK | guardrails | validates **content** (are inputs/outputs compliant) |
| Google ADK | Tool Confirmation | intercepts **execution** (should this tool run) |
| **LangGraph** | **interrupts** | **modifies state** (inspect and modify graph state at any execution point) |

⚠ **But be clear about what it explicitly does not give.**
The official docs mention no file-system permission model, network access control, or tool-level allowlist.

Compare OpenHands on our site (an explicit Docker sandbox + API-key mechanism)
and the Codex SDK (three `SandboxMode` enum values in source) —
**on the permission-boundary dimension, no official mechanism can currently be found for LangGraph.**
sections.选型必读：它和 Deep Agents 是上下层，不是两个选项:
This is a relationship we must untangle for readers, or they will double-count.

The official homepage's first screen carries a TIP pointing to Deep Agents:

> If you're looking to quickly build agents, check out **Deep Agents**
> — a **higher-level package built on LangGraph** for agents that can
> plan, use subagents, and leverage file systems for complex tasks.

**In other words: Deep Agents is a higher-level package built on LangGraph.**

| | LangGraph (this entry) | Deep Agents (also listed by us) |
|---|---|---|
| Positioning | low-level orchestration framework | batteries-included harness |
| Abstraction | explicit graphs, supersteps | agent + preset tools |
| File system | **not its business** (README files it to the upper layer) | core selling point |
| Subagents | express them yourself with the graph | preset |
| Memory | checkpoint + memory, two mechanisms | persistent memory + summarize |
| Fits | long flows, precise recovery, human state modification | wanting speed, wanting full features |

**One-line rule**: want to draw the flow yourself, want precise recovery → LangGraph.
Want less wiring, want ready-made capability → Deep Agents (it runs on LangGraph).
sections.工具与文件系统：它明确不管:
- **File system**: the only related sentence on the official homepage recommends Deep Agents as the upper-layer package
  ("leverage file systems for complex tasks") — **file capability belongs to the upper layer, not the graph engine**.
  What LangGraph gives is a **state container** (checkpoints store graph state).

- **Tool system**: none of the five capabilities is a tool system. Tools connect via the LangChain ecosystem.

⚠ We **do not associate LangGraph with the 9 servers on our MCP site**. There is no evidence LangGraph ships an MCP client.
sections.溯源与生态：它借鉴了谁:
The Acknowledgements at the end of the official homepage are informative:

> LangGraph is inspired by **[Pregel](https://research.google.com/pubs/pub37252/)**
> and **[Apache Beam](https://beam.apache.org/)**.
> The public interface draws inspiration from
> **[NetworkX](https://networkx.org/)**.
> LangGraph is built by LangChain Inc, the creators of LangChain,
> but **can be used without LangChain**.

**"can be used without LangChain".** This line is our key evidence that it is not hard-bound.
Model access usually goes through LangChain, but you can skip it.

(Pregel is Google's graph-computing paper — the source of the large-scale graph computation approach behind Beam.)
sections.版本号：踩过一个坑，请注意:
⚠ **Our test: `releases/latest` is unreliable for this monorepo.**

`gh api repos/langchain-ai/langgraph/releases/latest` returns
**`cli==0.4.32.dev0` (a subpackage dev build)**, not the main package version.

The correct approach is to list recent releases and pick the main package yourself.
Result of this verification (2026-10-01):

| tag | release date | note |
|---|---|---|
| `cli==0.4.32.dev0` | 2026-09-23 | subpackage dev build, **not the main package** |
| `cli==0.4.32` | 2026-09-23 | subpackage |
| **`1.2.12`** | **2026-09-21** | **← main package, used by this entry** |
| `sdk==0.4.5` | 2026-09-21 | subpackage |

In this monorepo, subpackage tags are named `<subpackage>==<version>`; the unprefixed one is the main package.
sections.核验说明:
Basis for `confidence: partial` (downgraded from verified on 2026-10-03):

> **Why downgraded**: the "unknown items" list still contains evidence gaps whose subject is **our site**
> (e.g. "conflict semantics of multi-process concurrent writes to the same thread", "interrupts re-entry boundary",
> "commercial terms of the LangSmith companion") — no longer the "official docs don't provide it" kind.
> Per the v3 rule "say unknown when unknown", marking verified would be inflated — downgraded to partial.
> **2026-10-08 re-verification**: short-term memory trimming (Trim / Delete / Summarize),
> long-term memory (store semantic search + content filtering), `langchain-mcp-adapters`,
> and "usable without LangChain" — these four have moved out of the gap list.

- ✅ Verified: repository existence and star count (43,731 · rolling verification 2026-10-23), license (MIT, via license API),
  > last push (2026-10-22, still active), full official homepage (positioning, three core capabilities,
  > the Deep Agents layer relationship, Pregel/Beam/NetworkX lineage, can be used without LangChain),
  > the "save graph state at every superstep" wording in `libs/checkpoint/README.md`,
  > the 9-subpackage list under `libs/` (`checkpoint`, `checkpoint-sqlite`, `checkpoint-postgres`,
  > `prebuilt`, `cli`, `sdk-py`, `sdk-js`, `checkpoint-conformance`, etc.),
  > 6 releases entries (including the tested record that latest is unreliable)
- ⚠ Not verified and **the official docs do not provide it** (not our gap): tool system, file system,
  > model provider list — we record these honestly as
  > "outside its remit" rather than "couldn't find it"
- ⚠ Not verified and **our gap** (the direct basis for partial):
  > the performance cost of superstep persistence, the interrupts re-entry boundary,
  > conflict semantics of multi-process concurrent writes to the same thread (not stated officially),
  > the concrete storage backend of long-term memory, commercial terms of the LangSmith companion, capability parity between the Python and JS/TS versions

runs:
This site has not completed measured runs. The test protocol is at [protocols/framework/_protocol.md](../../../protocols/framework/_protocol.md).

**Suggested runs** (tailored to orchestration framework + persistence dimensions):

| # | What to test | Why it is worth testing |
|:--:|---|---|
| 1 | Kill the process mid long-flow; does recovery truly resume from the interruption point | "exactly where they left off" is an explicit official promise — must verify |
| 2 | **Write overhead of superstep-granularity persistence on long tasks** | the official docs say every superstep is saved; with many steps the I/O cost is unknown |
| 3 | Conflict behavior of the Postgres checkpointer under multi-process concurrency | our biggest worry, unverified |
| 4 | Graph re-entry behavior after interrupts modify state mid-run | the official docs say you can modify agent state; the boundary is unverified |
| 5 | Actual cost of short-term memory trimming (Trim / Delete / Summarize) in long sessions | the official docs give the techniques; the cost is unverified |
| 6 | Code-volume difference: minimal LangGraph example vs Deep Agents for the same need | quantifies just how "low-level" the self-assessment really is |
unknowns:
- Write-conflict and recovery semantics of checkpoints across machines / multi-process concurrency
- Performance and write-volume cost of superstep-level persistence
- The concrete storage backend of long-term memory (the official docs give only the store abstraction, no named backend)
- The re-entry boundary after interrupts modify state
- Free quota and commercial terms of the LangSmith companion (quotes not recorded per our D9 rule), and whether LangGraph is fully usable without it
- Capability parity between the Python and JS/TS versions
related: **Same company, a layer relationship, not competitors**: the README states plainly that Deep Agents is a higher-level package built on LangGraph (with planning, subagents, file systems). Ready-made vs foundation — this is the comparison table our readers most need to see.

**A contrast within the orchestration family**: both are graph-execution orchestration frameworks; ADK gives Workflow Runtime + state management, LangGraph gives checkpoints persisted every superstep.
Also an orchestration framework, different center of abstraction (roles/tasks vs graph nodes).
Opposite form: that one is single-agent primitives + built-in guardrails; this entry is a low-level graph engine + state persistence, and provides no tool system.
